item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Tigers have given out a lot of bad money over the past few decades, whether it came in the form of free-agent contracts or extensions that didn’t turn out. Unfortunately over the past decade or two, we have quite a few to choose from.
You will see familiar, frustrating free-agent signings like Jordan Zimmermann, Victor Martinez, Mike Pelfrey, and Mark Lowe, to name a few obvious ones.
Many of them come from the recent past, as Al Avila’s time helming the franchise resulted in more than a few big misses.
But not all of them do. Scott Harris, while setting up the Tigers with a roster good enough earn a spot in the playoffs in back-to-back years, is not above making a few mistakes of his own.
There may be a few surprises from a little further back, too, as it’s not as if Dave Domrbrowski were totally perfect himself. And the losing Tigers from the 1990s didn’t often spend much money, but still managed to make a few high-profile whiffs of their own.
Before we dive in, a big thank you to stories at Bless You Boys, Vintage Detroit, and here at Motor City Bengals for being valuable resources that made researching and thinking about the list so much easier.
Now, let’s re-live some of the worst free-agent contracts in Detroit Tigers history.
20. Francisco Liriano, 2018
- 1 year, $4 million
- 0.3 WAR
Our list admittedly begins with some one-year deals, starting with Francisco Liriano’s. While this wasn’t a particularly painful contract in the grand scheme, former Twins star Liriano didn’t do much during his time in Detroit.
He did lose a lot, going 5-12 with a 4.58 ERA. He made 26 starts, 27 appearances total, and the Tigers lost two out of every three times he appeared on the mound for them.
He was worth a positive figure in WAR after eating about 133 innings on the mound, but that’s about the best you could say. It could have been even worse: he put up a 5.11 FIP.
19. Adam Everett, 2010
- 1 year, $1.55 million in 2010
- 0.3 WAR, 31 games, 89 plate appearances, .468 OPS, -3 DRS
Can you get upset over a small contract that just didn’t turn out particularly well? That was the question about Adam Everett’s deal as much back in 2010 as it is today.
Everett signed as a free agent with the Tigers for a $1 million deal in 2009. Known for his defensive prowess, he was kind of the epitome of an all-glove, no-bat player and put up 9 DRS (defensive runs saved) while batting .238 with .288 OBP and .325 slugging. Fans were frequently frustrated at how inept he was at the plate.
What especially inflamed them, however, was the fact Detroit brought him back again in 2010 after narrowly missing the 2009 playoffs by dropping Game 163 to the Twins.
He didn’t last long: just 31 games and 89 plate appearances. The Tigers released him on June 15 the 2010 season as he was batting .185 with .468 OPS. Worse, he was worth -3 DRS at the time, erasing the only positive reason for keeping him in the lineup.
The Tigers went on to finish a disappointing third place in the AL Central that year and not working to find a better shortstop in the offseason is at least partially why.
18. Eric Davis, 1994
- 1 year, $3 million
- -0.3 WAR, 37 games
On rare occasions in the 1990s did the Detroit Tigers give fans something to be excited about. They were, in fact, the losingest franchise of the entire decade. Generally, the team went into every year with little chance of making the playoffs and the only question would be which of their top players would be donning another team’s jersey by the end of the year.
In 1993, however, they caught fire early in the season and were fully 17 games above .500 and in first place in late June. Things soured a bit from there, but an August winning streak put them back into contention, so they made a trade with the Dodgers for star center fielder Eric Davis. They ultimately missed the playoffs (though did win an impressive 85 games that year), and David put up a .904 OPS during his time in Detroit. Combined with his time in LA, he finished the season with 35 steals to go with 20 home runs. So they decided to bring him back on a two-year deal.
It did not go well. He played just 37 games in the Tigers uniform in the strike-shortened 1994 season. He decided to retire and was granted free agency in October of 1994. He finished the contract with a .183 batting average and .582 OPS.
Only in the spring of 1995 did Davis learn from his doctor and announce was battling cancer. He eventually returned to baseball in 1996 and played for six more years. That’s certainly something to cheer on and feel good about in the end, but yet ultimately it’s hard to see his 1994 season in Detroit as anything but a failure.
You can read more about Davis’ time with the Tigers from Dan Holmes at Vintage Detroit.
17. Fernando Viña, 2003-04
- 2 years, $6 million
- 0.6 WAR (seems high!), 29 games, .226 batting average, .577 OPS
The 2003 Detroit Tigers were not just bad, they were historically bad. The fact they “only” lost 119 games can be attributed to winning five of their final six games of the season, two in walk-off fashion.
That’s kind of a hard sell to make to any free agent when trying to put together a better roster for the following year. While owner Mike Ilitch famously did manage to nab future Hall of Fame catcher Ivan “Pudge” Rodriguez by opening his checkbook in a huge way, he and President and General Manager Dave Dombrowski looked for more improvements to be made.
One they landed on: two-time Gold Glove winner and free agent second baseman Fernando Vina, who was not without risks after missing all but 61 games in 2003 with a hamstring injury.
Vina was signed to a two-year deal worth $6 million. It did not go well for either party. Vina played in just 29 games, hitting .226 with .557 OPS and. He did, however, put up 6 DRS, which was about the only thing that saved him from putting up a negative WAR during his time in Detroit.
He never made it past the month of May of that year, and his season ended when he decided to have knee surgery to repair torn cartilage. Later implicated in the Mitchell Report, Vina denied using steroids in 2003 but did admit to ESPN using HGH in an attempt to get back to full health.
16. Mike Moore, 1993-95
- 3 years, $10 million (5th highest paid Tiger in 1993)
- 0.8 WAR, 5.90 ERA (78 ERA+)
Mike Moore came to Detroit after spending the first 11 years of his MLB career on the West Coast. By the time he was a Tiger, he’d racked up 132 wins and a 1989 All-Star Game appearance. During his prior four years in Oakland between 1989-1992, he put up a 3.54 ERA (105 ERA+).
While injuries were not an issue for Moore like so many other of the failed contracts of this list, he was essentially not much more than an innings eater to close his career. In 1993, he started a league-high 36 games and threw more than 200 innings. While he put forth a winning record at 13-9, his ERA climbed to 5.22 (82 ERA+). Across 50 games to close the final two years of his time in Detroit, it only got worse. By 1995, he went 5-15 with a 7.53 ERA (64 ERA+). He was worth an amazing -1.5 WAR and finished his Tigers career with a 0.8 WAR.
15. Kenley Jansen, 2026
- 1 year, $9 million ($12 million team option for 2027 with $2 million buyout)
- 0.8 WAR, 4-6 record, 21 saves, six blown saves (78% save percentage)
Honestly, I would have expected Kenley Jansen's numbers to be worse. Every time he took the mound in a save or tie-game situation in the ninth inning or beyond, a pit started forming in my stomach. Not once did I think "this is a shutdown closer who can hold a lead."
Maybe ultimately that's why he deserves a spot on the top 20 list. Sure, there's probably some recency bias here. But what derailed the Tigers' 2026 season -- a season they were widely picked to win the division and make a playoff run -- was relief pitching. And Jansen did nothing to make the bullpen feel impenetrable.
14. Alex Cobb, 2025
- 1-year, $15 million
- Never threw a pitch
Alex Cobb is a hard one to rank. One the one hand, he was given a $15 million contract and never made a regular-season pitch for the Detroit Tigers. On the other hand, he didn't hurt the team with anything he did on the mound? So in the end this seemed as good of a spot as any to remember a Tiger who never really was.
He suffered a right-hip injury, saying the pain was so much it bothered him to walk, and has not pitched for any team since.
13. Mike Aviles, 2016
- 1 year, $2 million
- -1.5 WAR, 68 games, .210 BA, .528 OPS
While $2 million is a paltry figure, especially during the Tigers free-spending days of nearly a decade ago, and utiliyman Mike Aviles was never going to make or break the season, this contract makes the list just because of how badly it turned out.
Baseball-Reference put his WAR at -1.5 during just 68 games on the field for Detroit. FanGraphs was only a little bit more forgiving, going -1.1. No matter which you’d rather rely on or how insignificant the money spent, you can’t argue that bringing in a free agent only to have him send the team backward by more than a game is just a horrible signing all around.
Aviles made 181 plate appearances for the Tigers that year and hit .210 with .528 OPS. He had six extra-base hits, six RBI, and was caught stealing in 2 of his 4 attempts. His glove failed him too, making him as bad in the field as at the plate.
The Tigers finished in second place in the AL Central that year.
12. Prince Fielder, 2012-20 (traded before 2014)
- 9 years, $214 million. Traded after two years, $46 million paid. Gave Rangers $30 million for a total of two years for $76 million total cost.
- 6.9 WAR (4.7, 2.2) for Tigers, 55 home runs and .878 OPS
- Angered fans by saying, “It's not really tough, man. It's over,” after playoff loss.
Prince Fielder making the list summarizes what is ironically one of Detroit’s best and worst periods of baseball. The team repeatedly won the AL Central and seemed destined for the ALCS every year. Miguel Cabrera won the Triple Crown. Justin Verlander won the Cy Young. MVPs were a nearly expectation. Max Scherzer seemed to go toe-to-toe with Verlander in pitching prowess. In many ways it was one of the best runs during the history of the franchise – at least for anyone under the age of 50.
So it is unfortunate to include Fielder here, and a contract you could put in many different places on this list. From the day Prince Fielder signed with the Tigers, predictions were made about how it might turn out. Many of them foreshadowed the obvious: it might start well but it won’t end well. Little did they know how soon that would come to be true.
About two decades earlier, Tigers fans had had a love affair with Fielder’s father, Cecil. Back when 50 home runs was a bit number, Cecil’s run at the number in 1990 was a big deal. Prince grew up in the area when his father was a Tiger and played Little League ball in Grosse Pointe. Being able to get a “local” and the son of one of the most memorable Tigres players of the 90s was a big deal and so very fun.
It went well enough to begin. Across his two years in Detroit, Prince Fielder accumulated 6.9 WAR, hit 55 home runs and had an .878 OPS. The warning signs were there though, as his stats took a step backward for a third straight year.
In 2012, the Tiger made it to the World Series (where Fielder kind of fizzled, going 1-for-15) and they made it back to the ALCS in 2013 (where he again fizzled, going 4-for-22 with a double).
After the gut-wrenching ALCS loss, he told reporters, “It's not really tough, man. It's over. I got kids I got to take care of, I got things I got to take care of. It's over."
That was not what fans who had just had their hearts ripped out wanted to hear, and the negative backlash was fast to come.
Given the wrong-way production and the way everything was going off the field, moving Fielder out of Detroit was in the best interest of everybody. They sent him to the Rangers with $30 million for a package highlighted by Ian Kinsler.
Fielder played just 42 games the following season for the Rangers and only 289 total more before a neck injury forced him into retirement. The financial implications of that on the Tigers and Rangers were a bit more complicated. Nonetheless, even with the Tigers managing to dodge one by moving a large chunk of the contract off their payrolls, it’s hard to look at this deal as anything other than a big whiff in the end that could have been so much worse.
11. Anibal Sanchez, 2013-18
- 5 years, $85 guaranteed
- 1 good year, 3 awful
- 7.3 WAR
Let’s be serious. Some people are probably going to think Anibal Sanchez didn’t deserve to be on the list at all. Some people are probably going to think he could have been much higher up.
Sanchez had some absolutely amazing seasons in Detroit, notably the first year of this contract, and some absolutely awful ones. The awful ones are the reason for his inclusion.
Sanchez first came to the Tigers in 2012, along with Omar Infante, in one of GM Dave Dombrowski’s July trades that soon looked absolutely wonderful. While his regular season was somewhat pedestrian after the deal, going 4-6 with a 3.74 ERA, he shined in the postseason. Sanchez gave up four runs across 20+ innings and three starts.
Detroit rewarded him with a five-year, $80 million deal with an option for a sixth year the team could buy out for $5 million. It immediately looked like pure genius when he an American League-leading 2.57 ERA (162 ERA+) and finished fourth in Cy Young voting. That made him worth 6 WAR no matter the statistical source. A steal at $8.8 million that season.
The rest of his time in Detroit didn’t go so well. Held to 22 starts in 2014 due to injuries, he pitched just 126 innings with a 3.43 ERA. That was still good for 2.3 WAR, though he was paid $15 million that year. In 2015, he made 25 starts for a 4.99 ERA. In 2016, 26 starts at a 5.87 ERA. In 2017, six starts (17 games) at a 6.41 ERA. During that span his WAR had been worth a combined -1.2 while he earned $48 million. The Tigers saw enough at that point and paid him another $5 million in 2018 to decline the option.
Naturally, he bounced back with the Braves the following year and won a World Series with the Nationals after that, as Detroit is not allowed to have anything good happen.
So while the life of the contract may not look horrible, it’s hard to say he contributed anything positive to the team during the final three years of the somewhat pricey deal.
10. Kenny Rogers, 2008
- 1 year, $8 million
- 0 WAR, 5.70 ERA (78 ERA+), 9-13 record
As a hard-nosed 41-year-old, Kenny Rogers was a veteran leader and key reason the Tigers went from zeroes to heroes in 2006. That magical year, he won 17 games, posted a 3.84 ERA, pitched more than 200 innings and ultimately finished fifth in American League Cy Young voting. He made three starts in the postseason without giving up a run – though not without controversy about what exactly may have been on his hand.
It took a toll, limiting him to just 63 innings in 2007 after he was forced to undergo left shoulder surgery before the season even began.
The Tigers brought him back for one last hoorah in 2008 on a one-year deal, but sadly it did not go much better. Rogers did bounce back to make 30 starts that year, but he finished 9-13 with a 5.70 ERA (78 ERA+). All in all, it was an $8 million deal resulting in replacement-level play. The Tigers lost eight of his last nine starts that year.
9. Troy Percival, 1993-95
- 2 years, $12 million
- -0.2 WAR, 5.76 ERA (75 ERA+)
Troy Percival had many fine years as an elite closer. By the time it was over, he racked up 358 saves and 781 strikeouts while limiting his ERA to 3.17. During his last year with the Angels, he saved 33 games and finished the year with a paltry 2.90 ERA. This is not the Troy Percival the Detroit Tigers ended up signing for $12 million across two years.
Percival ended up pitching in just 26 games total during his Tigers career. He saved eight of 11 games that year, but was anything but a shutdown finisher by then. He missed most of the month of May due to injury. Upon returning, he was not the same. From June 11 to July 9, the Tigers watched as his ERA crept up from 2.93 to 5.76. In his final appearance as a Detroit Tiger, he gave up two runs in the bottom of the ninth to the then-Devil Rays to blow the game.
Percival was diagnosed with a “partial tear of his right flexor pronator muscle mass” – a forearm injury – that kept him out the rest of the year and the next. At one point, it appeared as if he were headed for retirement.
He ended up returning to baseball in 2007 with the Cardinals and closing his career out with a final two years with the Rays.
8. Mike Pelfrey, 2016-17
- 2 years, $16 million. Traded to White Sox after one year, Tigers pick up $7.46M of it.
- -0.1 WAR, 5.07 ERA (84 ERA+)
The 2016 offseason was just an unfotunate one in so many ways, with Al Avila stepping up to the general manager role and beginning a long number of unfortunate years for Tigers fans. Many of his first contracts handed out, even a few that sounded like a good at the time, went south on him.
Pelfrey signed a two-year deal worth $16 million in 2016. He made 22 starts with a 5.07 ERA and a 4-10 record. He never made it out of spring training in 2017, being released on March 30 of that year. The White Sox signed him, where he was actually even worse than he was in Detroit – but the Tigers picked up most of the cost.
7 Jack Flaherty (2026-2027)
- 2 years, $36 million
- 0.7 WAR, 11 wins, 4.62 ERA
Maybe bringing a player back after a trade isn't so good after all. Jack Flaherty was shipped to the LA Dodgers at the trade deadline in 2024. The Tigers went on to make the playoffs anyway. The Dodgers went on to win the World Series. And when it was all said and done, Flaherty signed a two-year deal to return to Detroit. It seemed like a great thing.
It never really turned out to be, however. Flaherty never regained what made him a fun player in 2024, going 8-15 for Detroit in 2025. He battled injuries a bit in 2026 and made 19 starts, going 3-8 for an 11-23 record. That actually puts his WAR per $ on this deal at 50 -- among the worst on this list. Only the relatively smaller dollar figure keeps this contract from looking worse compared to some players above him.
6. Framber Valdez, 2026-2028 (mutual option for 2029)
- 2026-2027: 2 years, $65.6 million. 2028: $35 million player option. 2029: $40 million mutual option, $5 million buyout
- 1.6 WAR
Framber Valdez is a new addition to this list in 2026. One year in he's cost a little shy of $23 million while providing just 1.6 WAR while providing 10 wins across 31 starts with a 4.01 ERA. Maybe that's not so bad in today's numbers on its face value. But he will earn $43 million next season, with a $35 million player option the year after. That is worrisome.
So we're going to begin in the top 10. If he has a great season in 2027, maybe it's closer to 10. If he has a terrible season, maybe he's just outside the top three. He controls his own fate here.
Still there doesn't seem to be much reason to be optimistic. This is his worst season in seven years, and he's 32 years old. The best is likely past him.
It also turned out to be a period of contracts where seemingly none of them would turn out well and taken together they helped choke the life out of the organization.
All in all, it went terribly.
5. Mark Lowe, 2016-17
- 2 years, $11 million
- -1 WAR, 7.11 ERA (60 ERA+)
Mark Lowe was another problem on a 2016 team that somehow won 85 games despite their offseason mistakes. Unlike Pelfrey he came to the team as a reliever. He pitched in 54 games, totaling 49.1 innings, but somehow put up a 7.11 ERA during the course of the year.
At one point after giving up five runs on June 18, Lowe’s ERA rose to 10.71. The kindest thing you can say is at least he didn’t lose a lot of games, going 1-3. Generally he was saved for lost causes to begin. The Tigres went 21-33 in games he appeared.
Mark Lowe was released from the team March 26, 2017, paying him $5.5 million to go. He never pitched in the major leagues again.
4. Joe Nathan, 2014-15
- 2 years, $20 million
- -0.3 WAR
- 4.78 ERA
What is more memorable about Joe Nathan’s time in Detroit? The great disappointment he became after joining the club to shore up a perennially shaky bullpen, or the chin flick heard ‘round Tigertown? At least you can laugh about the latter choice. Maybe.
Rather than the bullpen savior, he blew seven saves and put up an ERA of 4.81 in 2014. His strikeouts per nine innings dropped. His walks per nine increased by 50%.
The frustration for both sides peaked on Aug. 14, 2014, when he threatened to blow an 8-4 lead to the Pirates. Fans enthusiastically booed. Nathan replied with a chin flick, which is roughly Italian for something we can’t print on this site. The relationship was never really fixed despite a later apology.
In 2015, he made exactly one appearance, picking up a save on Opening Day. A torn UCL that game ended his season and Tigers career. Whether he would have rehabilitated his reputation by staying healthy that year will never be known.
3: Javy Baez, 2021-2027
- $116 million spent 2021-2026, $24 million due
- 3.3 WAR per Baseball Reference
Javy Baez is going to have a strange legacy in Detroit when he plays his last game. Financially the contract is awful. I debated a lot about where exactly this should land. In the end, it was just a terrible contract. But Baez did restore his legacy enough that unlike many players around him on this list he will likely be remembered more fondly as a player than the financials suggest he should be.
The results that first year could charitably be called a wash -- 2.4 WAR (per Baseball Reference) across 144 games played for Detroit. It quickly fell off after that.
Baez's defense waned slightly, and his reputation for chasing bad pitches was seemingly on display nightly. He failed to record even 1 WAR in 2023 and actually played worse than replacement level in 2024, causing many fans to just want to move on entirely at that point. Detroit paid about $47 million to get below-replacement results over the two year period.
The Javy Baez Renaissance Tour began in 2025 and slightly redeemed a terrible contract by finding opportunites for Baez to play important roles in games. While still financially in the metaphorical red on the deal, that was a bit of a victory. Fans' boos turned to cheers more often than not.
Still, another sub-0 WAR season in 2026 put his total at about 3.3 WAR at a cost of $116 million, or about $38.7 million paid per 1 WAR. Ouch.
2. Jordan Zimmermann, 2016-20
- 5 years, $110 million
- 2 WAR, 5.63 ERA (80 ERA+) in 99 games
You could look back on this deal with 20/20 hindsight and proclaim it to be doomed from the start. One of Al Avila’s worst deals, one of the worst contracts the Tigers ever handed out. But that’s only after Zimmermann suffered injury problems relatively early in his Tigers career. Before that, he was one of the top free-agent pitchers of that offseason. It’s just hard to remember that now.
Zimmermann came to the Tigers with a 3.32 ERA in Washington across seven years, having earned two All-Star team roster appearances and top-10 finishes in Cy Young voting twice as well. He even threw a no-hitter as well.
After earning the accolade of being named the Opening Day starter for Detroit, things went downhill. Zimmermann first hit the IL (then DL) in May with a groin strain. In July he was again out of action, this time due to his neck. He finished the year with a 4.87 ERA and 9-7 record.
In 2017, he managed to make 29 starts but went sub-.500 with an 8-13 record and an ERA that exploded to 6.08, the highest of his career at the time.
In 2019, it got worst when he went 1-13 with a 6.91 ERA. He made just two starts in 2020 before injuries again took a toll. He grand totals as a Tiger? 25-41 record and 5.63 ERA.
1. Victor Martinez, 2015-18
- 4 years, $68 million
- -2.1 WAR
Let's briefly note here that although Martinez was already a Tiger at this point, this was not an extension. Martinez was a free agent at the time of the deal, so we've opted to include it.
Like so many Tigers careers in the past decade or so, something that started off positive and good only leaves you with bad memories in the end. That is also the case with Victor Martinez.
When Martinez came to the Tigers from the Red Sox, it was a huge deal, and he became a fan favorite right away – and not just for the adorableness of his son, “Little Victor.” He put up a 138 OPS+ during those first three years with 58 home runs and 289 RBI.
Rewarded with a four-year contract following the 2014 playoff disappointment (Martinez had an .871 OPS in contrast to others earlier on this list and career-best .974 OPS during that regular sason), the 35-year-old DH was bound to disappoint by the end of it.
Unfortunately the disappointment didn’t take long. Martinez’s average dropped to .245 with .667 OPS in 2015. A bounceback 2016 season gave some hope, but over the final two years of the deal he hit for just .672 OPS. Not what you’re looking for from a designated … hitter.
He was worth negative WAR every year of the deal. Ultimately, it’s just a bad idea to give an aging DH a lengthy deal no matter how good he was for you in the past.
Updated September 24, 2026

item.title: [fultonsun.com] Skenes closes underwhelming season with start against Cardinals | Fulton Sun
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.description: Paul Skenes will make his final start of a disappointing season as he tries to lead the Pittsburgh Pirates to a win this afternoon against the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive contest of a three-game series. Skenes (10-11, 3.91 ERA) will attempt to help the Pirates (80-78) secure their first non-losing season since 2018. It would be only their second non-losing mark since 2015, which was the last time they made the playoffs. Pittsburgh is playing its home finale. The 2025 National League Cy Y
item.content:encoded:
Paul Skenes will make his final start of a disappointing season as he tries to lead the Pittsburgh Pirates to a win this afternoon against the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive contest of a three-game series.
Skenes (10-11, 3.91 ERA) will attempt to help the Pirates (80-78) secure their first non-losing season since 2018. It would be only their second non-losing mark since 2015, which was the last time they made the playoffs. Pittsburgh is playing its home finale.
The 2025 National League Cy Young Award winner will oppose Cardinals right-hander Kyle Leahy (10-5, 3.65) as St. Louis (77-81) tries to win for the third time in four games. The Cardinals need to prevail in all four of their remaining games to avoid a second straight losing season.
Skenes has seen his ERA nearly double from the 1.97 he posted last season, while his fastball velocity has dipped from 98.1 mph to 96.8 mph.
This week, Skenes stated he thinks pitching for Team USA in March during the World Baseball Classic may have contributed to his drop in fastball speed and his struggles this season.
“Usually, that time of year, you’re kind of ramping up and it’s a little bit slow. You can kind of get onto the slope and find your body,” Skenes said. “One live (batting practice), you’re topping at 97 (mph), and then the next you’re 98, 99. And that wasn’t the case this year. … Looking back, I don’t think that really helped.”
Skenes had a stretch of nine starts from May 17-July 1 during which he went 0-6 with a 5.36 ERA and the Pirates lost every time he pitched. During his past 13 starts since then, Skenes is 4-3 with a 4.31 ERA across 71 innings, with Pittsburgh going 8-5 in that span.
The 24-year-old LSU product gave up five runs on six hits, including two home runs, over six innings last Friday against the Kansas City Royals in his most recent start. He struck out seven and walked one in a no-decision.
Skenes is 0-5 with a 2.74 ERA in seven career starts against St. Louis. In his lone outing against the Cardinals this season, in Pittsburgh on April 30, he allowed five runs (three earned) on seven hits, including two home runs, while striking out nine and walking none in five innings.
The Cardinals, who clinched the season series against the Pirates with their 5-1 win Wednesday, will look to finish with eight wins in 13 meetings against their National League Central rivals.
Leahy, who has been on an innings limit of late, is coming off one of his poorer outings of the season. He gave up seven runs (six earned) on five hits and three walks and struck out only one in three innings during a 9-1 loss last Friday to the Washington Nationals.
“It’s disappointing. I didn’t make a lot of great pitches,” Leahy said. “I’m going to go through my bullpen with intent to get better as I always do.”
Leahy has not pitched more than three innings in any of his past five starts, with the Cardinals going 1-4 in that stretch. He doesn’t have a win since Aug. 18.
Leahy is 2-0 with a 2.12 ERA in nine career appearances against the Pirates. Both of his starts against Pittsburgh occurred this year. He fired 5⅔ innings of three-run ball at Pittsburgh on April 28 to earn a win, then threw three innings of one-run ball in St. Louis during a no-decision Aug. 29.

item.title: [New York Post] The Post’s top 30 looming MLB free agents
item.dc:creator: Jon Heyman
item.description: Contrary to popular opinion, the free agent market doesn’t consist of only one player. Yes, superstar starter Tarik Skubal will grab headlines since there’s nobody close. But while it may be seen as a one-man show, there are some other decent starters and useful position players. Here’s our top 30. 1. Skubal: MLB’s consensus top pitcher will almost surely beat Gerrit Cole’s $325M pitching record, which makes the Mets and incumbent Dodgers early favorites. He’s maintained his stuff following arth
item.content:encoded:
Contrary to popular opinion, the free agent market doesn’t consist of only one player. Yes, superstar starter Tarik Skubal will grab headlines since there’s nobody close. But while it may be seen as a one-man show, there are some other decent starters and useful position players. Here’s our top 30.
1. Skubal: MLB’s consensus top pitcher will almost surely beat Gerrit Cole’s $325M pitching record, which makes the Mets and incumbent Dodgers early favorites. He’s maintained his stuff following arthroscopic elbow surgery (“Skubal scope”) with a 2.95 L.A. ERA. It’ll be interesting if MLB’s salary cap desire affects things.
2. Bo Bichette,* INF: It’s certainly no guarantee he’ll opt out of $84M over two years (minus the unique $5M bonus for opting out) after an unremarkable year in Queens and yet another opt-out chance. But it’s a weaker free agent field, and the Phillies reportedly offered $200M over seven years last winter. They should have infield openings with Luis Arraez and Alec Bohm also free agents.
3. Randy Arozarena, OF: He timed his career year well, joining AL MVP Yordan Alvarez as the only players to post a 125 wRC+ every month, via MLB Network. Seattle needs Arozarena, whose clutch gene surfaced in the 2020 postseason.

item.title: [MLB.com] Skenes says his best baseball is still ahead after consecutive 200-K seasons

item.content:encoded:
Fast forward a season later, on the same date, Skenes fought to keep his ERA under 4.00 in his final start. Skenes finished a bumpy 2026 on a positive note, allowing one run in 6 1/3 innings in the Pirates' 2-1 win over the Cardinals in Thursday afternoon's home finale at PNC Park.
Skenes logged a 3.82 ERA and 200 strikeouts in ‘26, becoming the first Pirates starter with consecutive seasons of 200-plus K’s since Bob Veale (1964-66).
“It was a grind. It was definitely a grind,” Skenes said. “I think it was a good year. I don’t think it was to the caliber of the last two years, but I’m not gonna sit around all offseason thinking about how bad this season was, because I just don’t think that’s true.
“I understand the standard that was set the last couple of years, but I think there was a lot of good, and stuff to get better at. Probably some low-hanging fruit and some other stuff to address in the offseason, but the thing that I’m happiest about is the 32 starts.”
St. Louis took the lead on Skenes in the top of the first with a solo homer by Alec Burleson. After Burleson’s shot, the Pirates (81-78) tied the game in the bottom half of the inning on a single by Brandon Lowe. A stalemate then took place throughout the afternoon.
Skenes mowed down Cardinals batters, recording eight strikeouts and allowing three hits and two walks. He induced soft contact, and even played some defense to turn a 1-6-3 double play to end the fifth inning.
As he trotted out for the sixth with 81 pitches, Skenes retired the side in order. He then came out for the seventh at 90 pitches, and one strikeout away from 200. Skenes told manager Don Kelly that he felt the best he has in a long time, but Kelly didn’t want him over 100 pitches. Skenes took down Leo Bernal for his 200th K before being lifted in favor of reliever Yohan Ramirez with the game knotted at 1.
Skenes has been fairly open about the struggles in 2026 compared to his first two seasons, as his ERA nearly doubled with a dip in velocity. He was proud of grinding out 32 starts, and he learned plenty about his controllables going forward.
“We've talked a lot about nobody expects more from Paul Skenes than Paul Skenes expects from himself,” Kelly said. “I know what everybody sees every day is the same guy. Comes in, focused, works his butt off. And it was tough for him going through that. I think any time any of us go through anything that's tough in life, we learn from it, grow from it, and there's no doubt that Paul is going to as well. He has this year. I think today was evidence of that, just finishing on such a strong note, throwing the ball extremely well. Excited for him this offseason and excited for what he's gonna be next year.”
Skenes analyzed the idea of an 11-month season, saying he’ll begin throwing again likely near the end of October. A mental breather is needed, sometimes even more than a physical one.
The road was bumpy. Skenes has heard the clichés of being better off after facing adversity. He definitely doesn’t think it will hurt. But he won’t know if 2026 is an anomaly until he’s back on the mound in an MLB game once again.
“I think my best baseball is ahead of me and I think our best baseball is ahead of us,” Skenes said. “Got a long offseason and have the chance to sit down and look at all the stuff. It’s really easy to get emotional and kind of let emotions bleed into some stuff during the season. To be able to sit back and kinda look at the big picture rather than the day-to-day, short-term view of it that takes over in-season, that will be good.”

item.title: [tsn.ca] Rangers down Mets to ensure tie for AL West lead heading into final series of season
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.description: ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Josh Jung and Corey Seager homered, Kumar Rocker pitched five solid innings and Texas closed out its home schedule with a 3-1 win over the New York Mets on Thursday that ensured that the Rangers would remain at least tied for the AL West lead heading into the regular season’s final weekend. Texas (79-80) stopped a three-game losing streak and moved a half-game ahead of Houston, which played Thursday night at the Athletics. The Astros (78-80) hold the head-to-head tiebreak
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Josh Jung and Corey Seager homered, Kumar Rocker pitched five solid innings and Texas closed out its home schedule with a 3-1 win over the New York Mets on Thursday that ensured that the Rangers would remain at least tied for the AL West lead heading into the regular season’s final weekend.
Texas (79-80) stopped a three-game losing streak and moved a half-game ahead of Houston, which played Thursday night at the Athletics. The Astros (78-80) hold the head-to-head tiebreaker with the Rangers.
Texas, which finishes the regular season with three games in Minnesota, went ahead to stay on Jung’s two-run homer in the first inning off rookie left-hander Zac Thornton (5-6). Seager snapped an 0-for-15 skid when he led off the sixth with his 19th homer.
Rocker (6-11) struck out four while allowing one run and three hits. Jordan Montgomery, the fourth Rangers reliever, worked a perfect ninth for his second big league save. He’s made 161 starts and 17 relief appearances over nine big league seasons.
Francisco Lindor led off the game with a double and scored on Carson Benge’s two-out single to put New York up 1-0. Benge has a Mets rookie record 160 hits.
Thornton struck out four and walked one in his five innings. He allowed four hits and the only runs he surrendered were on Jung’s 12th homer. Seager went deep off Jefry Yan, another rookie.
Jung, who finished with three hits and a walk, is hitting .341 (15 for 44) in 11 games since coming off the injured list Sept. 12. He missed 47 games because of a left calf strain.
Up next
New York (73-86) goes to Washington (75-84) to open a three-game series Friday matching the two teams at the bottom of the NL East standings.
Texas plays Friday against the Twins, who never trailed while sweeping three games in Texas in mid-June.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here
Stephen Hawkins, The Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. – In a season with 11 walk-off victories, 35 come-from-behind wins, 31 usages of an opener, and countless defied expectations, the White Sox clinched their first playoff berth in five years on Thursday with a drama-free 9-1 blowout of the last-place Royals.
After a week full of pondering season-series tiebreakers and which stragglers in the American League Wild Card race needed to lose to enable the Sox to clinch, they entered Thursday afternoon with a much clearer mandate: win, and they would be in. Even with the division race against the Cleveland Guardians going down to the wire, guaranteeing postseason baseball of any stripe was plenty of incentive.
“I haven’t popped bottles or anything in a while and you never know when you’re going to have a chance to do it again,” outfielder Andrew Benintendi told the Sun-Times before driving in a pair of runs on Thursday. “Obviously we want to win the division. Hopefully we can pop twice in the next four days.”
And with that, the Sox offense jumped all over Royals starter Randy Dobnak for six runs in the first two innings of a game that never was in doubt. The mildly eyebrow-raising decision to start rookie David Sandlin without an opener produced six innings of one-run ball with a career-high seven strikeouts.
It was only this April that the Sox snapped a 14-game losing streak at Kauffman Stadium, yet the mistakes that historically marked their struggles in Kansas City were occurring on the other side.
After Sam Antonacci led off the game with a single, Dobnak’s throw on a Kyle Teel bunt attempt dragged first baseman Vinnie Pasquantino off the bag, helping to key a three-run first. The same story played out an inning later. Antonacci followed a Braden Montgomery leadoff single with a walk, and Dobnak compounded the problem with a quick pickoff move to first, only to find that Pasquantino wasn’t holding the runner nor expecting a throw. Montgomery scored all the way from second as the ball rattled around in foul territory, kickstarting another three-run frame. When longtime Sox villain Salvador Perez lined a solo home run in the fourth, it only made it a 8-1 game.
Each of the top-three hitters in the Sox lineup reached base at least three times. Antonacci scored thrice on the afternoon, Teel blasted his fifth homer of the year out to center in the fourth, and reigning AL Player of the Week Miguel Vargas both scored and drove in a pair of runs.
No team in MLB history has ever made the playoffs immediately after three consecutive years of 100 losses or more, until these 2026 White Sox pulled it off with three games to spare. That means there’s plenty of work to be done, as Thursday’s win pulls the Sox within a half-game of the Guardians in the AL Central standings. But there’s also plenty to celebrate.
“Obviously, we’ll continue to do our jobs,” said Davis Martin, the longest-tenured player on the team. “But it means the world today.”

item.title: [El Fildeo] Moreno y Arráez empatan en el liderato de bateo de la Nacional
item.dc:creator: Irinea Funes
item.description: El béisbol tiene una forma particular de escribir sus historias más bonitas: a veces, la pelea más emocionante no es entre rivales de distintas naciones ni de distintas generaciones, sino entre dos compatriotas que se persiguen en la cima. item.content:encoded:
El béisbol tiene una forma particular de escribir sus historias más bonitas: a veces, la pelea más emocionante no es entre rivales de distintas naciones ni de distintas generaciones, sino entre dos compatriotas que se persiguen en la cima. Eso es exactamente lo que está pasando en la Liga Nacional, donde Gabriel Moreno acaba de conectar su jonrón número 16 de la temporada para elevar su promedio de bateo a .312 y empatarse nada menos que con Luis Arráez en el liderato ofensivo del circuito. Dos venezolanos. Un solo trono. Y toda una temporada por delante para decidir quién se lo queda.
El golpe que lo cambió todo
Que un receptor lidere el departamento de bateo en las Grandes Ligas ya es, de entrada, una rareza que merece detenerse a contemplar. La posición de careta es, históricamente, la más exigente del cuadro: el desgaste físico, los turnos al bate interrumpidos por los cambios de entrada y la carga defensiva hacen que los números ofensivos de los receptores suelan quedarse por debajo de los del resto de la alineación. Por eso, cada vez que un catcher aparece peleando el título de bateo, la historia lo anota.
Moreno no solo aparece en esa conversación: la encabeza. Su cuadrangular número 16 no fue únicamente otro punto en el marcador, sino el empujón que lo colocó al nivel de Arráez, uno de los bateadores de contacto más consistentes del juego moderno. Que un jonrón haya sido el vehículo para alcanzar ese liderato dice mucho sobre la temporada completa que está teniendo el careta venezolano: no es un especialista de un solo recurso, sino un bateador que combina contacto y poder de manera que pocos en su posición pueden presumir.
Arráez, el obstáculo más difícil
Alcanzar a Luis Arráez en cualquier lista de bateo es mérito suficiente para encabezar una conversación. El también venezolano lleva años siendo uno de los porcentajes de contacto más altos de las Grandes Ligas, con una filosofía de bateo que parece diseñada específicamente para desesperar a los lanzadores: pocas ponchadas, muchos hits, un swing que rara vez regala outs.
Que ambos estén empatados a estas alturas de la temporada convierte cada turno al bate de los dos en un evento. Cuando Arráez conecta un hit, Moreno necesita responder. Cuando Moreno eleva su average, Arráez tiene que sostener el ritmo. Es el tipo de duelo que le da textura a una temporada larga y que los fanáticos del béisbol de verdad saben apreciar: no hay un villano ni un héroe forzado, solo dos peloteros extraordinarios empujando el uno al otro hacia lo mejor de sí mismos.
Por qué este duelo importa más allá de Venezuela
Es inevitable —y completamente válido— celebrar que el liderato de bateo de la Liga Nacional tenga acento venezolano de lado a lado. El béisbol de ese país ha producido generaciones de peloteros que han marcado el juego, y ver a dos de sus representantes actuales disputarse una corona individual en las Mayores es un recordatorio de la profundidad de ese semillero.
Pero el duelo Moreno-Arráez trasciende la bandera. Habla de dos estilos de juego distintos convergiendo en el mismo número: el receptor de poder que batea para average, y el especialista en contacto que no regala nada. Es una discusión táctica, histórica y estética al mismo tiempo.
- Gabriel Moreno demuestra que los receptores pueden ser fuerzas ofensivas de primer nivel, no solo guardianes del pitcheo.
- Luis Arráez sigue siendo uno de los argumentos más sólidos a favor del bateo de contacto en una era dominada por el poder y las ponchadas.
- La Liga Nacional tiene, en este duelo, uno de sus relatos más atractivos de la temporada.
¿Quién se queda con la corona?
Esa es la pregunta que vale la pena hacerse ahora mismo, con la temporada todavía en curso y los números tan apretados que cualquier racha —o cualquier caída— puede inclinar la balanza. El título de bateo no se decide en un jonrón ni en una semana brillante: se construye turno a turno, serie a serie, durante meses.
Lo que sí está claro es que mientras Moreno y Arráez sigan en esta pelea, la Liga Nacional tiene un argumento de primer orden para mantener los ojos puestos en ella. Y el béisbol venezolano, una razón más para sentirse orgulloso de lo que sus peloteros están haciendo en la cima del juego. La corona es de uno solo, pero el mérito, por ahora, es de los dos.

item.title: [amsterdamnews.com] Can the Yankees take down the Red Sox without Aaron Judge?
item.dc:creator: JAIME C HARRIS AmNews Sports Editor
item.description: This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced. item.content:encoded:
This was supposed to be the year the Yankees would win the franchise’s first World Series since 2009. A roster that included all-time greats Derek Jeter, Mariano Rivera and Alex Rodriguez, Hall of Famer CC Sabathia, and Series MVP Hideki Matsui, one of the best players Japan has ever produced.
Yet, as the Yankees look towards Tuesday, when they open the playoffs at home against what is virtually certain to be the Boston Red Sox, their longtime nemesis, in a best-of-three wildcard series, the prospects of them navigating an always perilous path to the World Series were reduced when Yankees manager Aaron Boone said this past Tuesday that the reigning American League MVP likely won’t play in the series due to a right calf strain.
“We’re planning on him not being a part of that,” Boone revealed to reporters.
Judge, who has only appeared in 66 games this season, primarily recovering from a right rib stress fracture, which caused him to sit out 84 games from May 31 to Sept. 8, is now on the 10-day injured list, placed there last Friday. The 34-year-old Judge, arguably the best player in the sport over the last decade, isn’t expected back for the divisional round if the Yankees get by the Red Sox.
Last weekend, Boone informed the media the team didn’t have a firm estimate as to when Judge, a three-time AL MVP, three-time AL home run leader, two-time MLB RBI king and last season’s MLB batting champion, would return to the lineup.
“I mean, I have no idea, we’re in the early stages,” expressed Boone, now in his ninth season as the Yankees manager. “We’ll just obviously treat it and see what transpires.”
The Yankees watched Tampa Bay clinch the AL East title on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium when they won the second game of a double-header on Tuesday 6-1. The Yankees shut out the Rays in the opener. Tampa Bay 96-61 going into the third game of the four-game series last night with the finale scheduled for 7:05 tonight. The Yankees were second in the division at 90-67 and the 84-73 Red Sox third.
With Judge unavailable, the Yankees offense will have to be multifaceted — both power and small ball will be required to make a deep postseason run. Designated hitter Ben Rice, who as of Wednesday had 39 home runs and 95 RBIs, both team highs, was the only Yankee with more than 20 homers and 80 runs batted in, so timely power will have to come from sources such as second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (19 home runs), first baseman Paul Goldschmidt (18), and left fielder Cody Bellinger (17).
But it is pitching that must advance the Yankees, led by leading AL Cy Young Award candidate Cam Schlittler, who is 14-6 with a 1.94 ERA and 234 strikeouts. Schlittler is scheduled to start tonight before taking the mound next week in the wildcard series.
But the prevailing question is: Can the Yankees win without Judge?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] ‘It Was a Grind,’ Pirates’ Paul Skenes Reflects on Perplexing Season

item.content:encoded:
PITTSBURGH – Paul Skenes' perplexing 2026 season came to an end on Thursday afternoon at PNC Park.
Skenes started against the Cardinals in his team's final home game of the 2026 season. The right-hander held St. Louis to one run on three hits with two walks and eight strikeouts in a 2-1 Pirates' win, their 81st of the season.
"He threw the ball great," said manager Don Kelly.
Skenes was at 90 pitches with seven strikeouts through six innings, but he trotted out back to the mound for one more batter in the seventh inning. Skenes struck out Cardinals designated hitter Leo Bernal, which gave him 200 punchouts on the season. He became the third pitcher in Pirates history to have two consecutive seasons with at least 200 strikeouts.
"I was pushing to go back out," Skenes said of chasing his 200th strikeout. "I think if I had gotten a strikeout in the sixth there, I wouldn't have gone back out. But I basically asked for one hitter and [Kelly] gave it to me. I appreciate that."
Skenes entered the season with high expectations after emerging as perhaps the game's top starting pitcher. But the reigning National League Cy Young winner fell short of the heavy standard he set through his first two years with the Pirates. Skenes finished his third big-league big season 10-11 with a 3.82 ERA in 32 starts.
Despite an ERA jump of nearly two full points, Skenes feels like he still had a good – albeit challenging – season.
"It was a grind. It was definitely a grind," Skenes said of his season. "I think it was a good year. I don't think it was to the caliber of the last two years, but I'm not gonna sit around all offseason thinking about how bad this season was, because I just don't think that's true. I understand the standard that was set the last couple of years, but I think there was a lot of good and stuff to get better at. … but the thing that I'm happiest about is the 32 starts."
A disastrous first start of the year on Opening Day in New York was quickly erased by a dominant stretch through the middle of May. Back-to-back eight-inning outings capped off a stretch of nine starts in which Skenes combined for a 1.09 ERA. But beginning with his start against the Phillies on May 17, Skenes combined for a 4.56 ERA over his final 23 outings. The Pirates went 9-14 in those games.
From his time in college at LSU to a brief stint in the minor leagues before his two-year dominance in the big leagues, Skenes had never gone through the adversity that he endured this season. While the results weren't always the same as what they've been, Skenes' consistency remained in his off-the-field work through the challenges.
"We've talked a lot about nobody expects more from Paul Skenes than Paul Skenes expects from himself," Kelly said of his ace. "I know what everybody sees everyday is the same guy. Comes in, [is] focused, works his butt off. And it was tough for him going through that."
Now that his season is over Skenes, will take time to shift his focus towards 2027. Despite taking a step back this season, he still feels like better days are ahead. And given the improvement the Pirates have shown this year, he feels the same way about what lies ahead for his team.
"I think my best baseball is ahead of me and I think our best baseball is ahead of us. Got a long offseason and have the chance to sit down and look at all the stuff. It's really easy to get emotional and kind of let emotions bleed into some stuff during the season. To be able to sit back and kinda look at the big picture rather than the day-to-day, short-term view of it that takes over in-season, that will be good."

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Jacob Misiorowski Just 1 Start Away From Brewers History
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy
item.description: Jacob Misiorowski is scheduled to take the mound one more time for the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season. If he gets through it without a blowup, he'll make Brewers franchise history in the process. Misiorowski is leading the league with an eye-popping 1.86 ERA in 169 1/3 innings of work. item.content:encoded:
Jacob Misiorowski is scheduled to take the mound one more time for the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season. If he gets through it without a blowup, he'll make Brewers franchise history in the process.
Misiorowski is leading the league with an eye-popping 1.86 ERA in 169 1/3 innings of work. Right now, the record for ERA in a single season by a Brewers starter is 2.36, which was set by Mike Caldwell back in 1978. Frankly, it would be difficult for Misiorowski to drop down and not break Caldwell's record at this point on Sunday in the Brewers' season finale against the St. Louis Cardinals. To put it into perspective, if Misiorowski allowed 10 earned runs on Sunday and didn't record an out, his ERA would increase to 2.39.
The odds of that happening aren't zero, but they're as close as you can get to it as possible. Even in the off chance that Misiorowski struggles, the Brewers could simply take him out if things aren't looking good.
History Is Coming For Jacob Misiorowski
So, on Sunday, Caldwell's record is likely to fall and Milwaukee will have a new single-season ERA champion. He has put himself in a position that guys like Freddy Peralta, Corbin Burnes and Brandon Woodruff never were able to. That's special. Burnes won a Cy Young Award in Milwaukee and his season wasn't anywhere near what Misiorowski has been able to do in 2026.
The closest player to Misiorowski in baseball in general has been Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees, who has a 1.94 ERA this season so far. The closest player to Misiorowski in the National League has been Chris Sale, who has a 2.16 ERA.
Last year, Misiorowski got the baseball world talking when he made his big league debut and flashed an elite fastball and made an All-Star Game sooner than everyone likely expected. This year, he has taken a massive leap and has been the most dominant pitcher in the league and has put together a season for the ages.
He got the ball on Opening Day for the Brewers this season and now the 24-year-old will bookend the campaign with history on the line. Sometimes, baseball can put together storybook situations you can't find elsewhere. This is yet another example. When the 2026 season began, there were questions about whether he could hold up for an entire season throwing as hard as he does. He has answered every question. Milwaukee is lucky to have him and if it is going to go on a deep run, the righty is going to be a significant reason why.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding "Milwaukee Brewers On SI," please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
Sep 24, 2026, 4:30 PM ET
Atlanta Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. (shin) is starting in right field and is batting second against the visiting Cincinnati Reds and right-hander Brady Singer on Thursday, per MLB.com. Acuna fouled a ball off his left shin in Tuesday's game against the Reds and did not start on Wednesday, but he is back for the series finale and should be returned to all starting fantasy lineups against Singer. In just five career at-bats against Senger, Acuna is hitting .600 with a solo home run. The 28-year-old former MVP and five-time All-Star had two separate stints on the injured list this year with hamstring injuries, which has limited his overall production for fantasy managers. Acuna has hit .259 (102-for-394) with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, 20 stolen bases, and 60 runs scored. Braves fans can breathe a sigh of relief that they did not lose Acuna just before the start of the playoffs next week, and they will be hoping he can carry over his hot hitting in September. In 19 games during the month, he has gone 25-for-74 (.338) with seven homers and 19 RBI in 81 plate appearances.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
More Recent News
Jesus Luzardo Throws Bullpen Session on Thursday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 4:14 PM ET
Philadelphia Phillies left-hander Jesus Luzardo (shoulder) threw a bullpen session that consisted of around 30 pitches on Thursday, as expected, according to Matt Gelb of The Athletic. Luzardo said the session went well. The Phillies could look to have Luzardo throw a simulated game this weekend to face live hitters, and he remains very much in play to return to the starting rotation for the start of the postseason next week in the wild-card series. The Phillies must first get into the postseason, as they entered Thursday tied with the Chicago Cubs for the final wild-card spot in the National League, with the Arizona Diamondbacks on their tails at three games behind with four left to play. Luzardo will be eligible to come off the 15-day injured list for the regular-season finale on Sunday, but he almost certainly won't be an option to pitch in that game as the Phillies look to save him for the playoffs. Getting the 28-year-old southpaw back for next week is the team's top priority after he went 14-5 with a career-best 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, and 221:52 K:BB in 178 2/3 innings across 29 starts in his second year with the organization.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Matt Gelb
Sep 24, 2026, 4:08 PM ET
The Chicago White Sox announced on Thursday that they placed right-hander Luis Castillo (shoulder) on the 15-day injured list with a right-shoulder impingement and recalled right-hander Tyler Davis from Triple-A Charlotte in a corresponding move. The White Sox had recently sent Castillo to the bullpen, but he did not fare any better there, posting a 13.50 ERA in three relief appearances after recording a 7.52 ERA in his final six starts of the year. The 33-year-old veteran Dominican will finish his 2026 regular season with a 4-11 record, 5.85 ERA, 1.49 WHIP, 112 strikeouts, and 44 walks in 130 2/3 innings across 29 appearances (23 starts) with both the White Sox and Seattle Mariners. Castillo was much worse in his nine outings (six starts) with the White Sox, recording an 8.42 ERA, 1.81 WHIP, and 26:12 K:BB in 31 innings. He will be eligible to return for the American League Division Series in the playoffs, but we have most likely seen the last of Castillo with the White Sox this year.--Keith Hernandez
Source: Chicago White Sox
Alex Bregman Has Resumed Hitting


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 3:23 PM ET
Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman (face) did not return to the starting lineup for the team's series finale against the Miami Marlins at Wrigley Field on Thursday, but he has resumed hitting, according to The Athletic's Patrick Mooney. The All-Star third baseman continues to recover from a freak accident when he was hit by a foul ball while in the on-deck circle against the division-rival Cincinnati Reds on Sunday. Bregman suffered multiple facial fractures, but manager Craig Counsell has not ruled him out from returning for the final regular-season series of the year this weekend at Fenway Park against his old team, the Boston Red Sox. "But he's feeling good in terms of the hitting part. That went well. He's happy with how that went, so we'll just do a little more, run around a little bit more today and see how that makes him feel. And we'll just keep progressing," Counsell said. To be cleared to play this weekend in Boston, Bregman needs to get the swelling down around his left eye. Bregman is hoping that his strong month of September (.295 average, .968 OPS in 18 games) can shift seamlessly into the start of the postseason next week, despite his freak face injury last weekend.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Patrick Mooney
Sep 24, 2026, 3:16 PM ET
Miami Marlins infield prospect Jacob Lombard's first taste of professional baseball was a mixed bag while playing for Single-A Jupiter. The Marlins' fourth-ranked prospect hit four home runs, stole 11 bases, and registered a 13.1 percent walk rate in 22 games for the Hammerheads. He also propelled the team to the Florida State League playoffs (which they went on to win) by hitting a go-ahead home run with the team down to its final strike of the season, then went 5-for-14 (.357) with a pair of home runs during the playoffs. The downside was that he hit just .220 during the regular season, due largely to an astronomical 39.4 percent strikeout rate. If the 2026 first-round draft pick can make progress in that area next season, he should see time at High-A and perhaps even Double-A by season's end. At just 18 years old, it will be a few years before he debuts in the majors, but there is plenty of upside here to make him a worthy stash in dynasty leagues.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Willson Contreras Won't Return in Series Finale


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 3:16 PM ET
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) is missing a sixth straight game in Thursday's series finale against the visiting Cleveland Guardians, per MLB.com. Nick Sogard is making another start at first base and will bat out of the leadoff spot against Guardians right-hander Daniel Espino. Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand in last Thursday's game against the Texas Rangers. X-rays came back negative, but Boston has elected to give him some extra rest with the postseason starting next week. We would expect Contreras to return during this weekend's series at home against the Chicago Cubs. The four-time All-Star has hit a career-high 27 home runs while driving in 81 runs in 129 games across 533 plate appearances, but he has only played in four games in September after hitting only .217 (18-for-83) with three homers, 11 walks, and 26 strikeouts in 23 games in August. The Red Sox will need Contreras, who has been one of their most consistent hitters for the majority of the 2026 season, in top form if they want to make a deep playoff run.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Ceddanne Rafaela Back in Boston's Lineup


Keith Hernandez




Sep 24, 2026, 3:10 PM ET
Boston Red Sox outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (hamstring) is starting in center field and batting sixth for Thursday's series finale against the visiting Cleveland Guardians and right-hander Daniel Espino, according to MLB.com. Rafaela returned from a stay on the injured list due to a quadriceps injury but was pulled on Wednesday night against the Guardians with tightness in his hamstring. An MRI exam on Thursday morning apparently ruled out anything concerning, and the power/speed threat and starting center fielder is back in action for the final game of the series at Fenway Park. It is great news for the Red Sox, who did not want to head into the start of the postseason next week without their starting center fielder. The 26-year-old will now have four games to try to set a new career-high mark in home runs, as he enters Thursday's action with 16 homers, 70 RBI, 17 stolen bases, 67 runs scored, and a .284/.319/.444 slash line in 536 at-bats this year. Rafaela was a first-time All-Star this year in his third full season in the big leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 3:06 PM ET
Miami Marlins outfield prospect Cam Cannarella tore through the Miami farm system this season on his way to Triple-A, logging just 19 games at High-A, then only 34 at Double-A before earning the promotion to the minors' highest level. Although his strikeout rate spiked from 12.9 percent at the lower levels to 23.8 percent while at Jacksonville, the Marlins' sixth-ranked prospect maintained a strong walk rate of 14.1 percent and still hit .282 with an .813 OPS to go along with three home runs and 11 steals in 45 games with the Jumbo Shrimp. In all, he hit 15 home runs across all three levels, not bad for someone who doesn't have a highly rated power tool, so it's something to keep an eye on in 2027. If the 23-year-old can continue to produce home runs to go with his penchant for contact and a keen eye, not to mention his plus speed, there could be a valuable fantasy asset here who would be on the verge of making his MLB debut next year.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 2:55 PM ET
Baltimore Orioles outfield prospect Ike Irish (knee) was enjoying his first full season of professional baseball earlier this year while playing for High-A Fredericksburg. The former first-round draft pick had really heated up before a torn left meniscus ended his season in late July. The Orioles' fifth-ranked prospect batted .361 with nine doubles, a triple, seven home runs, and nine steals over his final 26 games before the injury. The hot stretch pushed his season-long slash line to .286/.388/.528 with 16 home runs and 20 steals in just 76 games for the Keys. The left-handed hitter recently returned to the diamond and will head to the Arizona Fall League to make up for lost time. As such, he should be fully healthy come spring and looks ready to spend much of the 2027 season at Double-A. He likely won't make his major league debut until 2028, but the 22-year-old has shown good contact, plenty of power, and an ability to steal bases despite not having a ton of speed, so his dynasty arrow is pointing way up for the potential to impact multiple fantasy categories.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Liam Doyle Finishes 2026 on a High Note


Jarod Rupp




Sep 24, 2026, 2:37 PM ET
St. Louis Cardinals pitching prospect Liam Doyle capped off his 2026 season with a strong start in the Double-A Texas League Championship on Wednesday, allowing just one run (zero earned) on four hits and two walks while striking out six batters in five innings of work. It followed his earlier playoff start in which the left-hander gave up just one earned run on no hits and five walks while striking out eight batters in only 3 2/3 innings pitched. The former fifth-overall draft pick spent the entirety of the 2026 regular season at Double-A Springfield, recording a 3.76 ERA, 1.31 WHIP, and a 17.6 percent K-BB% in 23 starts (130 K in 103 IP). His performance this year puts the Cards' top pitching prospect on track for Triple-A in 2027 and a possible MLB debut at some point next year. If there is one criticism, it is that his walk rate remained elevated throughout the season, coming in at 12.5 percent, but so long as the 6-foot-2 hurler can keep striking out batters at a high clip, then it shouldn't get in the way of moving up the ladder. The 22-year-old remains a strong dynasty stash.--Jarod Rupp
Source: MiLB.com
Sep 24, 2026, 2:29 PM ET
Colorado Rockies corner infield/outfield prospect Charlie Condon capped off a strong 2026 season by smacking a home run in his final game of the year. item.title: [yardbarker.com] Mets fans won't love what Pete Alonso had to say about being an Orioles player
item.dc:creator: Zac Wassink
item.description: New York Mets fans repeatedly showed their love for Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso throughout the series between the clubs held at Citi Field earlier in September. Following the Orioles' 4-2 win over the Toronto Blue Jays on Wednesday night, Alonso offered a quote that sparked plenty of conversations on New York sports radio station WFAN and that may annoy some Mets supporters. "I believe in the baseball gods, and I honestly believe that, like, I'm here for a reason," Alonso said about pl
item.content:encoded:
New York Mets fans repeatedly showed their love for Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso throughout the series between the clubs held at Citi Field earlier in September.
Following the Orioles' 4-2 win over the Toronto Blue Jays on Wednesday night, Alonso offered a quote that sparked plenty of conversations on New York sports radio station WFAN and that may annoy some Mets supporters.
"I believe in the baseball gods, and I honestly believe that, like, I'm here for a reason," Alonso said about playing for the Orioles, as shared by Avi Carr-Gloth of WMAR-2 News. "I was always meant to be a Baltimore Oriole, and I think people are very appreciative and receptive to that, and I feel just as lucky and fortunate to be here as other people have told me. So it's special. That's really an understatement."
Alonso was a homegrown Met who played only for the club from when he made his MLB debut in 2019 through the 2025 season. Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns then controversially chose not to sign the franchise's all-time home run king to a long-term contract, and Alonso ultimately inked a five-year, $155M deal to join the Orioles.
While the 73-85 Mets spent the bulk of the summer knowing they had no chance of making the playoffs, Alonso slashed .264/.359/.512 with an .871 OPS, 41 home runs and 110 RBI over his first 159 games with Baltimore en route to becoming a potential American League MVP candidate. That said, the 78-81 Orioles began Thursday knowing they likely also won't participate in the postseason tournament.
"I know this hasn’t been the season that we wanted internally, and it’s not the season that’s expected internally," Alonso added on Wednesday night, per Andy Kostka of The Baltimore Banner. "The people who have supported us, it’s not what they expected or wanted either. For people to still show up, come out to a doubleheader today, and really just show the true support, it’s special, and that should be recognized."
If nothing else, Alonso's latest comments won't help Stearns' popularity among the Mets fans who chanted for team owner Steve Cohen to fire the executive before and after Alonso crushed his 300th career home run in Queens on Sept. 15.

item.content:encoded:
Jackson Holliday had an update on his surgery.
The Baltimore Orioles received more bad news on the injury front as their disappointing season winds down. Second baseman Jackson Holliday will undergo surgery on his left wrist later this week or early next week, ending his 2026 campaign, according to Jake Rill of MLB.com. “Hopefully just go in there and clean it up and that’ll be that,” Holliday added.
The recovery timeline runs about 10 weeks. That should leave Holliday plenty of time to be ready for the start of spring training in 2027. Manager Craig Albernaz also expects the infielder back at full strength by February.
The wrist issue caps a lost year for the 22-year-old former No. 1 overall pick. Holliday opened the season on the injured list after breaking the hamate bone in his right hand during spring training. He had several setbacks and did not make his debut until May 19. As a result, he spent nearly the entire year fighting through problems in both hands.
The numbers reflect that grind. Holliday hit .229 with a .300 on-base percentage and .640 OPS across 98 games. He added seven home runs, 30 RBIs and eight stolen bases. Holliday was slightly more productive in 2025. He played 149 games and posted 17 home runs, 55 RBIs and 17 stolen bases.
Still, Holliday has now logged three seasons in MLB and has never had a stretch where he lived up to the prospect hype. Time is running out for him to prove he deserves to be a part of this team’s future. Baltimore may even consider trading him away this offseason if the right package arrives.
Joining Holliday on the injured list is catcher Samuel Basallo, whose season also came to an end officially on Wednesday due to a concussion. Basallo took a foul tip off the mask during Monday’s game against the Toronto Blue Jays and later left the game.
Basallo had a promising first full season, batting .222 with a .291 on-base percentage, .696 OPS, 18 home runs and 54 RBIs.
They need a near-perfect finish just to stay alive. The club has already topped last season’s 75-87 mark, but they still have fallen short of expectations. The focus has now shifted to the offseason and a stronger push in 2027 with Holliday hopefully making a bigger impact.

item.title: [roundtable.io] MLB Shares Chris Sale Accomplishment During 3rd Atlanta Braves Season
item.dc:creator: Jesus Jimenez
item.description: Chris Sale has had a historic season for the Atlanta Braves. Atlanta Braves left-handed ace Chris Sale reached 200 strikeouts for the ninth time in his career on Wednesday night. MLB shared the accomplishment with a post on X. The 37-year-old veteran hit the mark in Atlanta’s 3-2, 10-inning walk-off win over the Cincinnati Reds at Truist Park. The milestone places Sale in company he has chased his whole life. He now joins Randy Johnson as the only left-handers in MLB history with nine 200-strike
item.content:encoded:
Chris Sale has had a historic season for the Atlanta Braves.
Atlanta Braves left-handed ace Chris Sale reached 200 strikeouts for the ninth time in his career on Wednesday night. MLB shared the accomplishment with a post on X. The 37-year-old veteran hit the mark in Atlanta’s 3-2, 10-inning walk-off win over the Cincinnati Reds at Truist Park.
The milestone places Sale in company he has chased his whole life. He now joins Randy Johnson as the only left-handers in MLB history with nine 200-strikeout seasons.
Sale needed just one strong night to get there in his final regular-season tune-up before the playoffs. He struck out 10 over 5 2⁄3 innings and surrendered only a lead-off home run to Juan Brito. He reached the mark in the sixth inning, catching Reds rookie Sal Stewart looking for punchout No. 200.
The outing capped a remarkable year. Sale finished the regular season with a 2.16 ERA, his lowest since 2018, to go with a 0.984 WHIP. He also had exactly 200 strikeouts across 162 2⁄3 innings and 27 starts. He had five double-digit strikeout games along the way.
His consistency stood out most. Sale made 17 starts with one walk or fewer and pulled off 24 straight starts allowing three runs or fewer, a franchise record. He was nearly unhittable every time he took the mound.
Acquired from the Boston Red Sox before the 2024 season, Sale won the National League Cy Young Award and swept the pitching triple crown in his first year in Atlanta. He will not win the award this year, but only because Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Jacob Misiorowski is having one of the best seasons ever by a pitcher.
Sale’s resurgence came after several seasons in Boston were derailed by injuries. He did miss time in 2025 due to a freak accident where he fractured his left rib cage.
Still, he has been the unquestioned ace of the Braves rotation since his arrival, which has mattered a ton given how many injuries the staff has dealt with.
Atlanta clinched the National League East on September 20, its seventh division title in nine years. The title came despite lowered preseason expectations with a new manager in Walt Weiss and their disappointing season in 2025.
At 93-65, the club has basically locked up the National League’s No. 3 seed and home-field advantage for a wild card series at Truist Park.
Sale is lined up to start the opener, likely Tuesday, in his first postseason appearance since 2021.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tigers Legend Justin Verlander’s Trade Advice to Tarik Skubal Revealed
item.dc:creator: Dominic Minchella; Unknown
item.description: The 2026 season didn't go the way that the Detroit Tigers would have wanted, with playoff aspirations and a Top 10 payroll to being sellers at the MLB Trade Deadline and finishing under .500. One of the biggest reasons Tigers fans were excited going into the year was the starting rotation put together. With the return of Justin Verlander, the signing of Framber Valdez and pairing both of them with Tarik Skubal, Casey Mize, and Jack Flaherty, on paper, the Tigers rotation looked to be one of the
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season didn't go the way that the Detroit Tigers would have wanted, with playoff aspirations and a Top 10 payroll to being sellers at the MLB Trade Deadline and finishing under .500. One of the biggest reasons Tigers fans were excited going into the year was the starting rotation put together.
With the return of Justin Verlander, the signing of Framber Valdez and pairing both of them with Tarik Skubal, Casey Mize, and Jack Flaherty, on paper, the Tigers rotation looked to be one of the best in the American League. But things fell apart quickly.
Eventually, both Skubal and Mize were traded to the National League, signaling another setback for Detroit. The biggest trade was Skubal going to the Los Angeles Dodgers, marking the first Tigers ace to be traded at the deadline since Verlander in 2017, when he was traded to the Astros.
Having created a bond in their short time in Detroit, Verlander and Skubal have reportedly kept in touch since the 2024/2025 AL Cy Young Award winner was traded to Los Angeles. Since that was his first time testing the waters on the other side, Verlander gave his former teammate some words of advice.
Verlander's Trade Advice to Skubal Revealed
Months after the trade, Verlander appeared on "On Base" with Mookie Betts as part of Bleacher Report to discuss the advice he gave Skubal before his move to the Dodgers.
"Getting traded is one of those things that you just really have to experience it yourself," Verlander told Betts. "I'm not really going to be able to prepare you for this except to say, 'It's like walking into a new school'.
"The only advice I had was: you get so stuck in your ways with one organization; it's nice to see something else, especially before free agency. You don't know what you don't know. You get more information, you meet new people, you experience the other side of the coin and I think that opens up a whole new world if you're open to it."
"We're both continuing to reach out; he knows I'm always here if he wants to pick my brain."
Verlander learned plenty after the trade from Detroit to Houston, securing two World Series championships and bonding with other All-Stars. Skubal looks like he's done the same in Los Angeles, posting pictures with his new teammates and celebrating a playoff berth.
The Dodgers and Skubal are heading to the postseason again after winning the NL West division, while Verlander is preparing to make his final start of his Major League career at Comerica Park this upcoming Saturday, Sept. 26, as the Tigers will cap off the 162-game season and sit back and watch.
Skubal's final start of the regular season is scheduled for Friday, Sept. 25, against the San Francisco Giants. Perhaps he'll have some time to tune in to the Tigers broadcast to watch Verlander pitch until his arm falls off one last time.
Dominic Minchella is a 2024 Eastern Michigan University graduate with a BA in Communications, Media, and Theatre Arts and a Journalism minor. He covers Major League Baseball for On SI and spends his free time watching games and sharing his insights.

item.title: [CBS Sports] The toughest players to rank at starting pitcher for 2027: Garrett Crochet's upside comes with major risk
item.dc:creator: Chris Towers
